overview: A cinematic journey through exile, justice, and the fragile act of return. Between courtrooms abroad and ruins at home, Ashes becomes a living archive: voices refusing disappearance, memories demanding recognition, and testimony transformed into resistance. More than a story of war, it asks an urgent question for Syrians and for the world: can justice and dignity be rebuilt from the ruins, or will silence prevail once more?

But Bella’s plea sparks an even more disturbing idea. Martha chooses not to kill her, instead, she devises a far crueler fate, one that strips Bella of control and dignity in ways she never imagined possible.
tagline: A plea for life turns into submission.

title: Cinema Impero
overview: Cinema Impero takes its name from the eponymous movie theater located in the center of Asmara, Eritrea, and built in 1937 during the Fascist regime. The video centers on a metanarrative that weaves together different spatial and temporal planes and various linguistic elements: materials drawn from the historical archive of Istituto Luce–Italy’s state-owned film company–and from the artist’s own private archive, recounted and interpreted by two voices and two intelligences. One artificial and one emotional. Cinema Impero is a black box, a device that encompasses cinematic, theatrical, and algorithmic languages. The work was originally presented as part a performance conceived for one viewer at a time. Placed at the center of historical macro-narrative, the individual spectator was confronted with a space of warm proximity to the artist, an intimate space of otherness shared between narrator and listener.

title: Youth Youth Youth
overview: Lorenzo Silvestri’s work often transfigures the relationships happening among his group of friends into paintings, garments, objects and moving images. Speaking about Youth Youth Youth, the artist explains: “When I was 10 years old, my father told me that his best friend as a young man had committed suicide wearing a suit, so that his parents would not have to pay for the funeral services to dress the body. From that day on, my idea of dressing up changed forever. I’ve had these images in my head for a long time and they eventually became a little film on loop. My intention was to create spokesperson images for everyone and make my loves and friends immortal”.

title: Endings: Nightclub
overview: Endings: Nightclub (2025) is a collaborative work by artist Marina Apollonio (Trieste, 1940), whose exploration of optical and kinetic art has been ongoing since the 1960s, and composer and sound artist Bottin (Guglielmo Bottin, Venice, 1977). Drawing inspiration from the hypnotic spiral movements that have long defined Apollonio’s practice—particularly her lacquered wood pieces, Fusione Circolare (2016) and Fusione Circolare Doppia (2019)—the video depicts a spinning vinyl record that embodies the dialogue between the two artists. The image captures the rhythmic expansion and contraction of black and white lines. Meanwhile, a fluorescent yellow turntable stylus, labelled Nightclub, traces the record groove from start to finish.

title: Gettin' Up

title: Above the Crocodiles
overview: Sonia Leimer`s video work Above the Crocodiles is based on archival footage recorded in 2002 by two Russian astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The filmic gaze from space onto various territories of Earth moves in a contingent search, brushing against geographical, ecological, and political contexts – conflict zones as well as everyday occurrences, casually commented on by the astronauts.

title: True Believers See More Patterns
overview: True Believers See More Patterns (2024) is a growing video archive of thylacine sightings, compiling all currently available footage sourced from online communities who believe the marsupial is still extant. The thylacine (also known as the Tasmanian tiger) was declared extinct in 1936, and its demise can be directly attributed to excessive hunting and habitat destruction caused by the establishment of the first British colonies in Tasmania in the early 1800s. Yet the animal seems to resist extinction by haunting the collective imagination. Entire online and offline communities have formed around blurry, slowed-down, and stabilized footage of alleged thylacines. Sightings continue, and large numbers are still reported today. The music by Turkish artist Cevdet Erek (Zincirli, 2021, Subtext Recordings, Berlin), performed in a single take on the davul, flows as an integral stream within the work, resonating with its open-ended nature.

title: Real Chernobyl
overview: Real Chernobyl attempts to reconstruct the movements and actions of Thomas Garenq, the man who sold the first footage of the Chernobyl disaster to the American TV networks ABC and NBC. The images produced by Garenq were later revealed to be fabricated and filmed on the outskirts of Trieste. In an effort to trace Garenq’s steps, the video revisits the sites of this fabrication: the Cattinara Hospital complex, the Melara neighborhood, and the hotel room in downtown Trieste where he stayed and negotiated with the networks. The video was shot in the summer of 2019—at the time, the hottest June ever recorded—against the backdrop of the emerging climate emergency, as TV networks aired the series “Chernobyl” and wildfires began to spread. Sound design and music by Alessio Dutto.

title: Littoral Formations

Her Mini DV archive can be seen as a proto-Instagram storytelling of a young girl growing up in southern Italy in the 1990s and early 2000s.

title: Never Ground
overview: Never Ground is inspired by science-fiction narratives of the subterranean world and by recent scientific discoveries that link speleological exploration to space exploration. The video unfolds as an uninterrupted loop depicting a descent and subsequent ascent through the entrails of a celestial body, tracing a potential space–time journey between the Earth and the subterranean passages of another planet.  In Never Ground, authentic ecosystems are seamlessly integrated with meticulously constructed studio settings, evoking the special effects techniques employed in pre-digital science fiction cinema—such as the use of miniatures sets and props.
